--- title: Datasets author: Marie-Hélène Burle --- :::{.def} While last section uses synthetic data, projects usually require real data. In this section, we look at three ways to obtain data: [Torchvision built-in datasets](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/datasets.html), [Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co/datasets), and your own data read with a custom class. ::: ## Our working dataset: EuroSAT Throughout this course we will use a single task: classifying satellite images by land use. [EuroSAT](https://github.com/phelber/eurosat) is a set of 27,000 small (64 × 64 pixels) RGB patches from [Sentinel-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentinel-2) images, each labelled with one of 10 land-use classes. It is a good fit for us: real research data (remote sensing), yet small enough (~90 MiB) to download and train on quickly, even on modest GPUs. It is distributed under an MIT licence (credit: [Helber et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1109/JSTARS.2019.2918242)). ## Packages ::: {#e600fd11 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from collections import Counter from pathlib import Path import datasets as hf import torch from matplotlib import pyplot as plt from PIL import Image from torch.utils.data import Dataset, random_split from torchvision.datasets import EuroSAT ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

When classes are heavily skewed, a high accuracy can hide a model that ignores the rare classes entirely; we will come back to this when evaluating models. ### Train and validation sets **Never evaluate a model on data it learned from.** We split EuroSAT, 80% for training and 20% for validation: ::: {#f94f180d .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} train, val = random_split( eurosat, [0.8, 0.2], generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(42) ) print(len(train), len(val), type(train).__name__) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

If they sit in one folder per class (exactly the layout EuroSAT uses on disk), a dozen lines give you a Dataset: ::: {#bb7052a8 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} class ImageFiles(Dataset): """Images in one subfolder per class under root; labels from folder names.""" def __init__(self, root, transform=None, extensions=(".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png")): root = Path(root) # sorted: alphabetical class names give deterministic, portable # label indices (the same convention as ImageFolder) self.classes = sorted(p.name for p in root.iterdir() if p.is_dir()) self.class_to_idx = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(self.classes)} self.transform = transform # scan the file list once (paths only: no image is read yet); # walking class by class gives ImageFolder's order self.samples = [ (path, label) for label, name in enumerate(self.classes) for path in sorted((root / name).iterdir()) if path.suffix.lower() in extensions ] def __len__(self): return len(self.samples) def __getitem__(self, index): path, label = self.samples[index] # convert("RGB"): one stray grayscale or RGBA file should not # crash a training run img = Image.open(path).convert("RGB") if self.transform is not None: # used on the preprocessing page img = self.transform(img) return img, label ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

Classes are sorted alphabetically, the same convention as `ImageFolder`, so label numbering matches. - `__getitem__` opens one image per call: decoding on demand is what will let worker processes parallelize the reading (next page). - `.convert("RGB")` prevents one stray grayscale or RGBA file from crashing training. - `transform` is the hook where preprocessing will plug in (a later page). Our section on [data preprocessing](../jxai/jxai_preprocess.qmd) in our [deep learning course with the JAX AI stack](../top_jxai.qmd) goes into this in a lot more details.
